evidence.reference_title: Imaging in bronchopulmonary sequestration.
evidence.snippet: Bronchopulmonary sequestration is an uncommon pulmonary disorder characterized by an area of non-functioning abnormal lung tissue, which receives its blood supply from a systemic artery and characteristically has no connection with the tracheobronchial tree.

nodes.description: A second account of how the intralobar form arises: the sequestered tissue grows from an accessory lung bud, is enveloped by normal lung, and keeps its own systemic arterial supply. A 1986 single-hospital pathology series gives this as the view generally held for the intralobar form, then proposes that most intralobar cases are something else; the authors of a case of bilateral intralobar sequestration joined by an isthmus suggested an origin from accessory lung tissue. No cached source shows the bud itself, so the node's edge sits in its own hypothesis group beside the bronchial-atresia account rather than replacing it.

evidence.reference_title: Intralobar pulmonary sequestration (a nonentity?).
evidence.snippet: Intralobar pulmonary sequestration has generally been considered a congenital malformation in which an accessory lung bud develops, is enveloped by normal lung, and retains its systemic arterial supply.

nodes.description: The defining vascular lesion. The sequestered tissue is perfused by a systemic artery, most often from the thoracic aorta and next most often from the abdominal aorta, instead of from the pulmonary artery. No bronchial artery supplies it.

nodes.description: The load the aberrant feeder places on the circulation. Neonates with large lesions are severely symptomatic and improve after the feeder is closed, and high-output cardiac failure is recognised often enough to be listed among the contraindications to surgery in a paediatric embolisation cohort. Which side of the heart takes that load differs between the two forms, so the entry does not state a shunt direction for the disease: the intralobar majority drains to the pulmonary veins and so returns to the left atrium, while the extralobar minority drains to the systemic veins. No cached source names a direction, and the subtype rows carry the drainage figures.

evidence.reference_title: Pulmonary Sequestration.
evidence.snippet: Pulmonary sequestration is a condition in which a segment or lobe of dysplastic lung tissue exists with no communication with the rest of the tracheobronchial tree and receives an anomalous systemic vascular supply, separate from the rest of the lung. It is, therefore, a nonfunctional tissue.

nodes.description: One of three accounts of how the lesion arises, and the one with a prospective pathological series behind it. An atretic lobar, segmental or subsegmental bronchus was found in every extralobar and in most intralobar sequestration specimens examined prospectively under a dissecting microscope, which would place this disease on a developmental spectrum with congenital pulmonary airway malformation and congenital lobar emphysema rather than apart from them. The accessory lung bud account is the Accessory Lung Bud node, whose edge has its own hypothesis group, and an acquired origin for the intralobar form is a third group.

evidence.reference_title: Bronchial atresia is common to extralobar sequestration, intralobar sequestration, congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation, and lobar emphysema.
evidence.snippet: Pathologic examination revealed atresia of a lobar, segmental, or subsegmental bronchus in 100% of ELS, 82% of ILS, 70% of CCAM, and 50% of LE (those clinically recognized to have BA or minor CCAM) cases.

evidence.reference_title: Bronchial atresia is common to extralobar sequestration, intralobar sequestration, congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation, and lobar emphysema.
evidence.snippet: It may be that both have the same etiopathogenesis with anatomic differences accounted for by aberrant genetic programs or other insults, perhaps modified by time of onset or duration.

nodes.description: The standard treatment. In a 97-patient adult series minimally invasive surgery beat open thoracotomy on blood loss, drainage volume, hospital days and drainage duration, with no perioperative mortality and complications in 4 per cent.

evidence.reference_title: Preoperative embolization of dual arterial supply in extralobar pulmonary sequestration: a case report and literature review.
evidence.snippet: Surgical resection is the gold standard treatment for PS.

evidence.reference_title: Pulmonary sequestration in adult patients: a single-center retrospective study.
evidence.snippet: Though no significant differences regarding operative time (P = 0.133), the minimally invasive surgery group was significantly better than the open thoracotomy group regarding intraoperative blood loss (P = 0.001), drainage volume (P = 0.004), postoperative hospital days (P = 0.017) and duration of chest drainage (P = 0.001).
